newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS--Grain futures soar on bullish USDA report.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS--Grain futures soar on bullish USDA report.

text.p: U.S. grain and oilseed futures markets soared on Friday after the U.S. Department of Agriculture cut its final estimates of 1996 crops and grain stocks and reported the lowest wheat plantings since 1978.

Chicago Board of Trade corn and soybean futures jumped their allowable daily limits at the opening bell with CBOT wheat and Kansas City Board of Trade wheat also up sharply. CBOT oats and Winnipeg canola also surged on the USDA news.
At 1030 CST, after an hour of trade, CBOT January soybeans were trading at $7.25 a bushel, up 29-1/4 cents.
March corn was at $2.65 per bushel, up 6-3/4 cents, after an early high at $2.70-1/4. March wheat was trading at $3.91, up 1-3/4 cents, after soaring early to $3.99-3/4.
"The biggest shocker of the report was the winter wheat acreage number, the lowest since 1978," said Dan Basse, analyst with Chicago-based firm AgResource Co.
Before the opening, the USDA in its monthly crop estimate said U.S. farmers seeded 48.2 million acres of winter wheat last fall for harvest during the early summer of 1997.
That seedings tally was sharply below an average of analysts' expectations for 51.4 million acres.
Basse and John Zanutto, senior vice president of LFG Futures, told reporters that most data of the government's final 1996 crop production numbers were bullish.
USDA pegged 1996 U.S. soybean production at 2.382 billion bushels, below average expectations for 2.407 billion.
It also lowered its estimate for 1996-97 U.S. soybean carryover stocks next September 1 to 155 million bushels from the previous outlook for 180 million.
"Securing bean supplies over the next few months will be difficult," Zanutto said, referring to the current posture of farmers to hold tight to remaining on-farm soybean stocks.
Cash grain dealers reported that a large processor had "pushed" its cash bid for soybeans after the report, telling farmers it would pay a bonus for quick sales.
"We're pushing our bids but haven't bought a thing. You never get any (business) when you do that," one dealer said.

USDA also pegged 1996 U.S. corn production at 9.293 billion bushels, below average expectations of 9.317 billion. The 1996-97 U.S. corn carryover stocks estimate was trimmed to 959 million bushels from the previous 1.157 billion bushels.
Despite the strong surge, analysts were cautious about predicting a prolonged rise in grain prices, however.
"We doubt rallies from the report can be sustained," Basse said. "The question mark here is, does the report change the long-term bearish picture."
Indeed, by mid-morning, commercial grain firms and some farmer selling in futures to cash in on the price surge was pushing grain futures off the highs, CBOT floor traders said.
Ray Halley, chief of USDA's crop branch in Washington, said low U.S. winter wheat seedings could prompt more plantings later this year of spring wheat.
"This is just winter wheat seedings...a lot of times when you see low winter wheat, you see more spring wheat plantings to fill in the void," Halley told reporters.

Fred Vogel, director of USDA's estimates division, also said that "it is a safe assumption" that more non-wheat crops will be planted this year because of the new "Freedom to Farm" bill that allows farmers more leeway in planting decisions.
